facts.text: In 1787, Evstratii Delarov, manager of the Shelikhov-Golikov Company, founded a trading post at Karluk, tapping nearby hunting grounds across Shelikof Strait.
The Ascension of Our Lord Russian Orthodox Chapel, built in 1888, blends Alutiiq and Russian traditions and was moved 80 feet inland in 2021 to escape bluff erosion.
Karluk’s weather is dominated by a strong marine influence, keeping precipitation moderate, clouds persistent, fog frequent, and freezing temperatures rare.
The Koniag Alutiiq, also called Sugpiaq, have lived on Kodiak Island for over 7,800 years, building a maritime subsistence economy around abundant local resources.
Karluk sits beside the Kodiak National Wildlife Refuge, home to roughly 3,000 Kodiak brown bears, with 180–200 concentrated in the Karluk Lake drainage.
Russian Orthodoxy, introduced in the 1780s, merged with Alutiiq customs, creating a unique cultural blend that persisted even after Alaska’s 1867 sale.
